pr.title: Run CI on the release pull request the Release workflow opens
pr.head: 66dabf1af4efa449ac0f2342056a91e6c2149ccd

summary: Field releases through a GitHub Actions workflow, .github/workflows/release.yml. You start it by hand, its propose job raises the version in package.json on a release/vX.Y.Z branch and opens a pull request, and merging that pull request is the decision to ship. The workflow opens the pull request with GITHUB_TOKEN, the token GitHub gives every workflow run.

GitHub creates CI's pull_request run for a pull request that GITHUB_TOKEN opened, but holds it until someone with write access clicks Approve workflows to run. That is what happened to the first release pull request, #207. This change makes CI start on every release pull request without that click: after the propose job opens the pull request, or finds one already open on a re-run, it runs gh workflow run ci.yml --ref release/vX.Y.Z. A workflow_dispatch run needs no approval, so ci.yml gains workflow_dispatch as a trigger, and the propose job gains actions: write, the permission a dispatch needs.

The held run still appears on the release pull request. The docs and the release pull request's own Testing text tell the reviewer to leave it unapproved, because approving it runs every CI job a second time on the same commit.

The change also documents the three levels at which an administrator must let Actions open pull requests (enterprise, organization, and repository), which the first release run ran into. The plan, docs/projects/install/readme.md §9.1, records both points, with the two alternatives the dispatch beat: approving the held run by hand, and a GitHub App token.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• GITHUB_TOKEN: the token GitHub gives each workflow run. Events it causes mostly start no further workflows.
  • workflow_dispatch: the event that starts a workflow on request, from the Actions tab or gh workflow run. A GITHUB_TOKEN dispatch starts a run with no approval.
  • Held run: a pull_request run GitHub creates in an approval-required state, shown as action_required, until someone with write access approves it.
  • Propose job: the Release workflow job that bumps the version and opens the release pull request.

cards.title: What happened on #206 and #207
cards.html:
• Release run 38167355504 failed its first attempt, because the enterprise did not let Actions open pull requests.
  • #206 was opened by hand from the pushed branch and closed a minute later. Its CI ran normally.
  • A re-run of the Release workflow opened #207 as github-actions[bot]. CI run 38167745651 was created four seconds later and ended action_required. A maintainer started its second attempt 22 seconds after that, and linux passed.
  • #207 merged at 19:25:19Z, and Release run 38167947880 tagged and released v0.2.0.

cards.title: Review history so far
cards.html:
• b294214: changes requested. The docs said GitHub starts no CI for the release pull request, when it holds a run for approval, and approving that run beside the dispatch would run CI twice.
  • 66dabf1: clean. All four passages describe the held run, the reviewer is told to leave it unapproved, and §9.1 records why the dispatch beat approving it.
  • Still open outside the diff: the pull request body's post-merge test still assumes #207 is open, and §9.2 and §9.3 of the plan still owe the first release, which shipped as v0.2.0.

groups.title: The release dispatches CI
groups.kicker: The propose job starts CI on the release branch, and CI accepts the dispatch.
intro: A workflow run cannot normally start another one: GitHub ignores most events that GITHUB_TOKEN causes, to keep workflows from triggering each other in a loop. A pull request that the token opens or pushes to is a partial exception: GitHub creates its pull_request runs but holds them for approval. A dispatch is a full exception, so the propose job ends with gh workflow run ci.yml --ref "$branch", on both of its paths: after it opens the pull request, and after it finds one already open on a re-run.

A dispatched run tests the tip of the release branch, which is the pull request's head commit, and GitHub records its checks on that commit. Because the dispatch reads ci.yml from the release branch, and that branch starts from main, it works only once this change is on main.

checks.text: CI's concurrency group is CI- plus github.ref. A dispatched run's ref is refs/heads/release/vX.Y.Z, and a pull_request run's is refs/pull/<n>/merge, so a dispatched run cancels an older dispatched run on the same branch but never a pull_request run.

files.note: Adds workflow_dispatch to the triggers, with a comment giving the reason.

checks.text: No job or step in ci.yml reads github.event_name or github.event.pull_request, so both jobs run the same steps under a dispatch. Checked by parsing the file and reading every job.

files.note: The propose job gains actions: write and ends with the dispatch. The release pull request body now says CI was dispatched, tells the reviewer to leave the held run unapproved, and describes released --since.

checks.text: actions: write is scoped to the propose job, which runs only on workflow_dispatch. The publish job keeps the top-level contents: write, and the repository default token permission is still read, read with gh api repos/okamnesiac/field/actions/permissions/workflow.
The heredoc renders cleanly with stand-in values, including the new sentence about the held run: every backtick is escaped, and only $version and $BUMP expand. Rendered locally from the parsed step.

No ${{ }} expression appears inside a run step. $branch comes from the version that scripts/release.ts bump prints, and it is quoted. Under set -euo pipefail, a failed dispatch fails the job after the pull request is open, and a re-run dispatches again.

groups.title: The release guide and the plan
groups.kicker: Why CI is dispatched, the three settings levels, and the plan record.
intro: docs/release.md is the guide to cutting a release. It now says that the workflow starts CI on the release pull request, why it dispatches CI rather than relying on the held pull_request run, and that the reviewer leaves the held run unapproved. It also names the three levels of Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests: the enterprise, the organization, and the repository. Each level must allow it before the one below can.

The install plan's §9.1, "What implementation settled" for chunk 2, records the enterprise policy that stopped the first release run, and the dispatch with the two alternatives it beat. The plan stays in-progress.

files.note: Step 2 now says the workflow starts CI. A new paragraph explains the held run and the dispatch, and the settings paragraph names all three levels.

checks.text: Matches GitHub's documented behavior and #207: CI run 38167745651's first attempt ended action_required, and its second, started by a maintainer, passed linux and windows. The two concurrency groups, CI-refs/pull/<n>/merge and CI-refs/heads/release/vX.Y.Z, differ, so approving the held run does run CI twice.

files.note: §9.1 replaces the repository-setting bullet with the enterprise policy, and adds the dispatch decision with the two alternatives it beat.

checks.text: The decision names both alternatives and why each lost: approving the held run by hand is a click on every release, and a GitHub App token needs an App and two secrets.

Run 38167355504 is real: its first attempt failed, and its second attempt opened #207. §9.2 still says the workflow has not run, and §9.3 still owes the first release, which shipped as v0.2.0. Those lines predate this change.
